prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We pass the straits of the Cape where grazing whales gather, though they’re not, I’m told, social creatures by nature. Alice asks how they can sleep if they must think to breathe. Cranial hemispheres wink and wake and alternate, so whales are half-awake and half-asleep, balanced between each of our states through dive and breach. Once on the kitchen wall of a dune shack I saw, like a headdress, the baleen of a whale— frayed filaments run from a thin, curled, rib-like bone: sieves for the sea. Like this sickle-moon fin “negatively buoyant” I sink in sleep, but end, I think, where I begin. Following one as it leaves two other whales we see suddenly not what we’re heading for but the asymmetrically colored snout of a fin whale as it rises parallel within a stone’s throw of the boat, the great eye set back water crashing rushing to let me see where it ought to be. I lose track, the mottled chin’s marble veined, swirling through its green veil, which the top jaw slits. And then, that’s it, I think. Nights I’m thrown upright from my rest. Brine thumps my chest.

Keywords: Cape, Alice, Cranial

outputs.L1:
We pass through the straits of the Cape, where grazing whales gather, though they are not, I’m told, social creatures by nature. Alice asks how they can sleep if they must remember to breathe. Their cranial hemispheres wink, wake, and alternate, so that whales remain half-awake and half-asleep, poised between our states through dive and breach.

Once, on the kitchen wall of a dune shack, I saw the baleen of a whale displayed like a headdress—frayed filaments extending from a thin, curled, rib-like bone: sieves for the sea. Like this sickle-moon fin, “negatively buoyant,” I sink in sleep, but end, I think, where I begin.

Following one whale as it leaves two others, we suddenly see not what we are heading toward, but the asymmetrically colored snout of a fin whale rising parallel to us, within a stone’s throw of the boat—the great eye set back, water crashing, rushing aside to let me see where it ought to be. I lose track: the mottled chin is veined like marble, swirling through its green veil, which the upper jaw cleaves.

And then, that’s it, I think. At night, I’m thrown upright from my rest. Brine thumps my chest.
outputs.L2:
We travel through the Cape’s narrow waters, where whales congregate to feed, although I’m told they are not naturally sociable. Alice wonders how an animal that must consciously breathe can ever rest. The two halves of its brain take turns shutting down and becoming alert, leaving the whale suspended between sleep and wakefulness as it plunges beneath the surface and breaks through it again.

In a shack among the dunes, I once saw whale baleen mounted on the kitchen wall like ceremonial headgear: ragged strands hanging from a slender, curved bone resembling a rib, a filtering net for seawater. In sleep, I too descend like this crescent-shaped fin, “negatively buoyant,” yet somehow finish, I believe, at my starting point.

We follow a whale as it separates from two companions. Then, without warning, our attention shifts from our destination to the unevenly colored muzzle of a fin whale surfacing alongside us, no farther away than a stone can be thrown. Its enormous eye lies farther back, and the water surges and tumbles aside, allowing me to glimpse where it should be. I cannot keep sight of it. Beneath a green curtain of water, its blotched chin twists like veined marble, while the upper jaw cuts through the surface.

And then it is over, I think. At night, I jolt upright from sleep, feeling salt water pound against my chest.

The speaker also remembers a piece of baleen, frayed at the edges like an ancient headdress. In life, this structure serves as a vast sieve, filtering food from the surrounding sea.

The encounter becomes immediate when a fin whale suddenly rises close beside the boat, moving parallel to it. outputs.L4:
Off Cape Cod, we watched the sea for the brief white burst of a fin whale’s breath. A whale does not breathe automatically as we do; each breath is a deliberate act. It must rise, open its blowholes, empty its lungs in a sudden plume, inhale, and descend again. Even in sleep, it cannot surrender entirely. One half of its brain rests while the other remains alert enough to steer the body toward air.

I thought about how strange such sleep must be—never wholly unconscious, never completely released from the demands of the body. Human beings sink into sleep as though into deep water, trusting the small machinery of the brain to keep the lungs working. A whale possesses no such trust. Its rest is divided and watchful. Depending on the air held in its lungs and the movement of its body, it may hover, drift, or slowly sink, then wake itself and rise.

The fin whale is immense, second in size only to the blue whale, yet it feeds on some of the smallest animals in the ocean. Instead of teeth, it has baleen: long, flexible plates that hang from the upper jaw like a dark curtain. The whale opens its mouth and surges forward, taking in a tremendous volume of seawater. Then it closes its jaws and forces the water out through the baleen, trapping krill and small fish against the fibrous fringe. Vastness sustained by what can scarcely be seen.

We had been following blows in the distance when one whale disappeared. For a moment the surface was empty. Then the water beside us changed.

The whale rose so close to the boat that there was no time to prepare for its size. Its back appeared first, dark and shining, an expanse rather than a shape. The blow came with a force I felt in my body. The air filled with the damp, animal smell of its breath. Beneath the surface, its mass continued far beyond what I could take in at once. I saw the curve of its body, the movement of water along its skin, and, for an instant, the eye.

It seemed impossible that an animal so large could approach without our noticing. The boat, which had felt substantial a moment earlier, became thin and provisional. The whale could have struck us accidentally, could have rolled beneath us, could have overturned our small craft with a movement that meant nothing to it. Yet it did none of those things. It passed with an eerie precision, close enough to make us feel both noticed and irrelevant.

Awe is not the same as comfort. I was astonished, but I was also afraid—not simply of the whale, but of the scale it revealed. The sea had concealed that body until the instant it chose to surface. What else moved below us, breathing deliberately, sleeping by halves, supported or abandoned by the water?

Long afterward, the encounter returned when I tried to sleep. As I lay in bed, breathing without thought, I would remember the whale rising beside the boat. I would hear again the explosive exhalation and feel the vast dark body passing just beneath the surface. Sometimes I became conscious of every breath I took, as if breathing had suddenly become my responsibility. Sleep, which should have been an act of surrender, turned watchful.

The whale remains with me in that borderland between waking and sleep: immense, silent, and suddenly near. I do not remember it as a distant shape on the horizon but as a physical presence—the smell of its breath, the wet shine of its back, the terrifying nearness of its weight. Each time the memory returns, I am again in the small boat off Cape Cod, waiting above deep water while something enormous rises to breathe.
outputs.L5: At Cape Alice, the sea crashed against the cliffs with a steady, thunderous rhythm. Alice stood near the edge, her cape twisting in the wind as she examined a weathered skull discovered among the rocks. Its cranial structure was unusual—smooth in some places, fractured in others—and hinted at a mystery buried by time. As the tide rose, Alice carefully wrapped the fragile object in her cape and began the long journey back to the village, unaware that her discovery would challenge everything the locals believed about the cape’s forgotten past.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about whale watching near Cape Cod, blending scientific facts about unihemispheric sleep, baleen, and buoyancy with dreamlike personal memories.
counterfactuals.output:
Off Cape Cod, the morning lifted slowly from the water, gray as the inside of a shell. Provincetown dwindled behind us—white steeple, dunes, the faint geometry of roofs—while the Atlantic breathed under the hull.

Then a humpback surfaced.

First the dark grammar of its back, then the blow: a brief cloud standing where no cloud should stand. I remembered my mother hanging sheets in a coastal wind, each one filling like a sail, each one collapsing around her body until she seemed to vanish and return. The whale, too, was always arriving from some other world.

Whales do not sleep as we do. One hemisphere of the brain rests while the other keeps watch, governing breath, listening for danger, guiding the body toward air. Sometimes one eye closes while the other remains open. I thought of all the nights of childhood when I slept beside the murmuring radiator, half-dreaming of tides, while some bright half of me stayed awake to hear my father come home.

The whale rose again, pleated throat expanding, mouth immense. From its upper jaw hung baleen—keratin, like our hair and fingernails—fringed plates that strain the sea. Water poured away; sand lance and herring remained, silver syllables caught in a dark cathedral. To eat, the animal gathered abundance by letting nearly everything go.

Gulls stitched cries into the wind. The naturalist called out distances, dorsal fins, fluke patterns, but the day kept loosening from names. Beyond Stellwagen Bank, light moved over the water like a hand searching a fevered forehead.

Buoyancy held the whales between descent and return: air in the lungs, the lift of blubber and body, the fine adjustments of motion and breath. Yet they sank with such grace, arching downward as if gravity were not a command but an invitation. I remembered learning to float in a kettle pond, my sister’s hands beneath my back. Trust the water, she said, though she was trembling too.

At last the flukes lifted—black, scarred, shining—and slipped under.

For several seconds nothing followed but the widening rings.

Still, I felt the whale below us, dreaming with half a mind, carrying its breath through the green dark, filtering hunger from water. And I stood at the rail with one eye on the empty sea, one eye turned inward, where my vanished family walked the Cape’s pale beaches forever—small figures in fog, buoyed by memory, surfacing whenever I remembered to breathe.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a first-person literary passage in which the narrator and Alice encounter a fin whale from a boat; use vivid marine imagery and end with the experience haunting the narrator’s sleep.
counterfactuals.output:
Alice saw the blow before I did—a white plume lifting from the iron-blue water, briefly luminous in the low sun.

“There,” she whispered, though the sea was loud around us.

The boat rolled in the long Atlantic swell, its hull creaking like an old rib cage. Kelp streamed past in olive ribbons, and gulls hung overhead, their cries sharp as torn metal. Then the fin whale surfaced beside us.

Its back rose without hurry, immense and dark, carrying a sheen of water that broke into silver runnels along its flanks. The sea seemed too small to contain it. For a moment I saw the pale, asymmetrical blaze of its jaw beneath the surface, one side ghost-white, the other lost in green shadow. Its breath reached us—warm, rank, astonishingly alive—and Alice gripped my wrist.

Neither of us spoke. The whale moved forward with the grave certainty of weather. No fluke lifted; only the long ridge of its spine passed under the waves until the ocean closed over it, smoothing itself with deceptive ease.

Yet below us, I could still feel it: a vast body traveling through the cold cathedral of the deep, beneath shoals flashing like coins and forests of drowned light.

That night, and for many nights afterward, sleep carried me back to the boat. I would hear Alice whisper *There*, feel the water rise beneath me, and wake with the whale’s dark back still rolling through my dreams.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental nature essay that shifts between whale biology, a remembered piece of baleen hanging in a dune shack, and the sudden close appearance of a whale beside a boat.
counterfactuals.output:
### The Mouth Is a Weather

A whale does not have to open its mouth to alter the sea.

Its body goes before it as pressure, a hill traveling under the skin of the water. Copepods rise and scatter. Herring turn, each fish reading the silver flank of the next. The whale’s heart, divided into four chambers like ours, contracts in the dark architecture of its ribs. Blood leaves the extremities. Lungs compress. The animal descends carrying oxygen not only in breath but in muscle, where myoglobin keeps it—redder than our red, a private store of night.

This is what the books say.

In the dune shack, a piece of baleen hung from a nail beside the door.

It was long, black-brown, and frayed at one edge, as if it had once been a giant’s broom. All summer it tapped the wall when wind came through the cracks. The shack stood beyond the last pitch pine, where the dunes began their slow migration inland, pouring grain by grain across the old road. Nothing there stayed where it had been put. Sand entered the bedsheets, the sugar bowl, the hinges of binoculars. In August, sand nested in my ears.

But the baleen remained on its nail.

Someone said it had washed ashore after a storm. Someone else said my grandfather had cut it from a dead whale, though by then he was dead too, and could be accused of anything. As a child, I thought baleen was bone. The word sounded skeletal: *bay-leen*, pale beams in a cathedral. I imagined it hard and white, holding the whale open.

It is not bone.

It grows from the gums in plates of keratin, the same structural material as fingernails, hair, hooves. On the inner edge, each plate breaks into fringes. A right whale swims through a bloom of plankton with its mouth open, water entering the enormous curve of the jaws and leaving through this hanging sieve. A humpback engulfs whole weather systems—krill, anchovies, seawater—then closes its mouth and presses the ocean out with its tongue.

What remains is swallowed.

What leaves has passed through a curtain.

*

The morning the whale came beside the boat, we had been looking elsewhere.

This seems important. The captain pointed toward a white disturbance half a mile off. Everyone turned starboard. Cameras lifted. A child in a red jacket shouted each time a wave broke, “There!” though there was nothing there, then nothing, then—

breath.

Not ahead of us.

Beside us.

The sound was less like blowing than a door kicked open in another room. A wet detonation. The air filled with fish-smell, salt, and something mammalian and warm. The whale’s back surfaced so close I could see water traveling across it in separate streams. Black, but not black: charcoal, blue slate, a bruised shine. Scars crossed the skin. Pale commas clung near the dorsal ridge.

The boat suddenly seemed invented.

Every screw, rail, orange life jacket, every posted regulation and molded plastic seat—all of it became flimsy and theoretical. The whale was not large in the way a building is large. A building stays where measurement puts it. The whale’s size moved. It continued under us.

Someone whispered, “Oh my God,” with no particular religion.

Then the eye appeared.

Or I remember the eye appearing. Memory improves an encounter by giving it a witness.

A whale’s eye is small relative to its body, positioned low and far back on the head. It does not offer the broad, forward attention of a human face. Yet beside the boat there was an eye, dark and oiled, and for one impossible second the animal seemed not merely visible but looking.

At us?

At the hull?

At the bright, trembling boundary between water and air?

The whale rolled. Its pectoral fin passed underneath, green-white in the depths, longer than a man laid end to end with himself. Then the body bent, and the sea accepted it without closure. No hole remained. Only the boat rocking in the muscular afterwater.

*

In the shack, I used to run my fingers down the baleen’s fringe.

It was surprisingly soft at the tips.

“Don’t,” my mother would say, though she never explained why. Perhaps it was dirty. Perhaps it was precious. Perhaps touching it disturbed some arrangement between the living and the dead.

At night the dunes pressed close to the windows. Wind moved over the roof in sheets. The baleen clicked against the wall: body without body, mouth without hunger.

I pictured the whale it came from.

Wrongly, of course.

I gave it teeth behind the plates. I gave it a cave for a stomach. I gave it the loneliness adults had already taught me to admire in whales—the lone singer crossing blue miles, calling into an empty world.

But many whales are not alone. Calves learn migration routes beside their mothers. Humpbacks coordinate bubble nets, spiraling beneath schools of fish and releasing columns of air that gather prey into a flashing concentration. Sperm whales—who have teeth, who dive into pressure-thick darkness—exchange patterns of clicks called codas. Different clans use different rhythms.

Even solitude, in the ocean, may be full of sound.

A blue whale can send a low call across distances that make the human idea of shouting absurd. The note travels beyond sight, beyond weather, perhaps beyond immediate need. The receiving whale may answer. It may not.

Communication is not proof against loneliness.

Nor is silence proof of it.

*

What I remember most clearly about the whale beside the boat is not the eye.

It is the skin.

There were scratches, mottlings, small topographies. Until then, I had imagined whales as smooth symbols: conservation, grandeur, depth. The animal that surfaced was marked by contact. Parasites had fastened to it. Teeth or rock or ice had written on it. Its surface carried the world.

The piece of baleen in the shack was like that too, though I did not know how to read it. Near its base, the plate was thick and polished. Toward the fringe, it divided into hundreds of fibers, each one catching dust. The whole apparatus had evolved to separate nourishment from flood.

A life depends on such separations.

Water from krill. Air from water. Memory from invention. Awe from the desire to possess what caused it.

The whale surfaced once more, farther away. A dark back lifted, lengthened, vanished. This time everyone saw it. Cameras clicked like insects.

Years later, the shack was taken down before the dune could take it. The cups went to one cousin, the iron stove to another. No one knew what happened to the baleen. Perhaps it was boxed in an attic. Perhaps it was thrown away by someone who thought it was a ruined broom. Perhaps possession was only another story we told about what had already passed through our hands.

I sometimes hear it still: a faint tapping in the night wind.

Keratin against pine.

The remnant of a mouth touching the wall.

And beside it, always, the sudden whale—rising so close that the scale of the world fails, exhaling the deep interior into our startled air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a dense, meditative piece of creative nonfiction about passing a cape crowded with feeding whales, combining factual observation with fragmented syntax, metaphor, and a sense of nocturnal panic.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk we rounded the cape and found the sea breathing.

Not figuratively. Not at first. White columns rose everywhere from the darkening water, briefly vertical, then bent by wind: exhalations of humpbacks, each warm plume collapsing into the cold air. The blows appeared ahead, abeam, behind us—an intermittent geography. The whales were feeding where the current struck the submerged shelf and lifted cold, nutrient-rich water toward the surface. Upwelling: the plain word for abundance summoned from depth. Plankton. Krill. Schooling fish turning as one silver organ beneath the hull.

The cape itself remained black and low, an animal refusing to name itself.

We throttled back.

A humpback surfaced close enough that I heard the intake after the blow, that deep unsealing. Its back emerged piecemeal, glossy with runoff, broader than our small understanding of it. No dorsal fin at first. Then the knuckled ridge. Then absence. The body continued below the surface, invisible but not gone, and this was the first instruction of the night: what disappears may still be beside you.

More whales. Cow and calf, perhaps. Solitary adults. Loose groups converging on food rather than one another. Humpbacks do not need a permanent pod to become, for an hour, a congregation. They gathered where the fish gathered. They lunged through the water with mouths open, pleated throats expanding to hold several tons of seawater. Baleen would strain the prey out afterward—the great mouth emptied of ocean, retaining only the small, bright lives.

A miracle with mechanics. A cathedral built around filtration.

Gulls tightened above them, shrieking. Shearwaters skimmed the troughs. The surface erupted in patches as fish fled upward from below, finding sky where safety should have been. The whales came under them. The birds came over them. Hunger arranged the world vertically.

Night advanced without color. The western seam closed.

Someone said there were twenty. Someone else said fifty. Counting became impossible because a whale could surface twice and become two whales in the mind, or surface once and remain everywhere. Blows ignited in the dusk. Flukes lifted, pale undersides briefly legible, each pattern of scars and pigmentation as individual as a fingerprint. One animal slapped its tail. The report traveled over the water and struck the chest before the ear.

Then panic, small at first.

Not fear of the whales. Or not exactly. Fear of scale. Fear of being placed correctly inside the dimensions of the world.

The chartplotter glowed at the helm. Our course curled around the cape in a thin electronic line, confident as a vein. Depth numbers changed. The radar swept. Green pulse, green pulse. Instruments insisting that location was possible while the sea erased every reference beyond the rail.

The engine idled unevenly.

Or I imagined it.

At night every ordinary sound enters the body wearing a mask. A loose cup in the galley becomes metal fatigue. A change in pitch becomes fouled propeller, failed fuel pump, flooded bilge. The hull shudders and the mind supplies the reef. The mind, industrious little undertaker, measures us for disaster.

No moon yet. No horizon.

Only breath around us.

Pffft to starboard.

Then another, nearer.

A whale’s exhalation can exceed three hundred kilometers an hour as it leaves the blowholes; moisture condenses in the colder air, mixed with mucus and seawater mist. Facts returned like handholds. Mammals. Voluntary breathers. They must surface. Their blood and muscles store unusual amounts of oxygen; their heart rate slows on the dive; circulation favors the organs that cannot wait.

They know darkness differently.

One surfaced beside the boat. The back rose like a road through rain. For several seconds it traveled parallel to us, carrying barnacles, scars, the accumulated punctuation of migration. Humpbacks may travel thousands of miles between high-latitude feeding grounds and warmer breeding waters, living between hunger and birth, between the cold pantry and the warm nursery. This one had crossed distances our fuel tanks could not imagine.

It breathed.

The sound was cavernous and intimate. A door thrown open in a house beneath the house.

I gripped the coaming. Absurdly, I thought of all the rooms in which I had woken after midnight convinced that death had entered—not dramatically, no hood, no blade, only a pressure in the chest, a skipped beat, plumbing ticking in the walls. The old nocturnal arithmetic: if I sleep, I vanish; if I remain awake, morning must arrive. As though vigilance were a rope tied to the sun.

Around the cape, the whales fed without reassurance.

Dive. Rise. Empty the lungs. Fill them. Descend again into what cannot be seen.

The sea kept making openings and closing them. Mouth. Blowhole. Wake. The brief white oval left by a fluke, called a footprint, remained after the animal sounded: smooth water marking where immense force had passed. We crossed one. The boat lifted almost imperceptibly.

Behind us the feeding continued, violent and exact. Fish condensed into bait balls. Whales circled and surged. Some humpbacks use bubbles to corral prey, releasing air below the school so a rising curtain encloses it. Nets made of breath. Walls with no substance. The prey bunch inward, away from the bubbles, and the whales ascend through the center, mouths widening into darkness.

To be trapped by air.

To be saved by air.

The cape fell astern. Its light appeared at last—a measured flash, then blackness, then flash. Not comfort, precisely. A rule. A repetition. Something keeping time while everything alive consumed or fled or surfaced because it must.

I watched until the last visible blow dissolved.

But even afterward, far into the night passage, I heard them where they were not: in the engine’s exhaust, in the rush along the hull, in my own breath returning too quickly. The body a small frightened vessel. The body a deep-diving animal ordered toward air.

Breathe, then.

Nothing solved.

Breathe.

The dark all around us, feeding.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
